note: Second follow-up on PR #180's stress-test findings (see 0200 for the first — NFC in the normalize seam). PR #180 filed 'pure-emoji strings normalize to empty and therefore collide on the empty key' as an observational finding whose Out of Scope explicitly named it: 'Fixing the emoji normalization finding (would require changing StringMatcher.normalize()).' This decision is that change. A mid-turn peer review from a Grok session (forwarded by the operator) reached the same diagnosis independently and pushed on the wider design question; the two deferrals below credit that input.

decisions.question: Should StringMatcher.normalize preserve emoji through the strip pass, so distinct emoji key distinctly instead of colliding on the empty string?
decisions.commitment: Yes. `nestor/matcher.py:191-235` iterates the NFC-folded input character-by-character and keeps any character that (a) matches the pre-existing `[\w\s]` set OR (b) has Unicode General_Category `So` (Symbol, other — most emoji: smileys, transport, weather, single-codepoint flags) or `Sk` (Symbol, modifier — skin-tone modifiers). Zero-width joiner (U+200D, category `Cf`) is still stripped, so a ZWJ sequence like 👨‍💻 normalizes to 👨💻 — non-empty, and distinct from other sequences. The `re.sub(r'[^\w\s]', '', text)` regex is gone; a compiled `_WORD_OR_SPACE = re.compile(r'[\w\s]')` and a `_EMOJI_CATEGORIES = frozenset({'So', 'Sk'})` module-level constant back the comprehension. Gated by 16 tests in tests/test_matcher_emoji.py (7 fix cases including ZWJ, skin-tone, multi-emoji ordering, and text+emoji integration; 5 must-preserve for currency, math, punctuation, Cyrillic-vs-Latin, ASCII byte-for-byte; the ∞-still-collapses case that documents the narrow scope; 1 idempotence sweep; 2 end-to-end integration through memory.add_pair / best_sealed including a prose-serve regression). All 177 tests in PR #180's tests/test_unconventional.py still pass, with the two locked emoji tests rewritten in place against the new invariant (test_emoji_only_stories_key_distinctly_after_0202, test_single_emoji_seal_distinctly_after_0202) and two docstrings updated to note the workaround is no longer necessary.
decisions.why: PR #180 filed this as an adversarial-shaped finding — 'homoglyph attacks and normalization edge cases' — but the failure mode is not adversarial: it is any real user storing emoji-keyed content who watches the second seal silently overwrite the first (the second key wins on the empty source_norm the unique-per-domain constraint keys on). The Grok peer review names the same shape: '🔥 started returning the 💀 translation'. The seat rule for changing normalize is 'the operator sees a character on their screen, and the store treats it the same way the operator does' — a strip pass that collapses every emoji to the empty string fails that bar for anyone whose keys use emoji. NFC (decision 0200) fixed the composition class of that same rule; this decision fixes the symbol-erasure class. What the historical strip pass stripped for non-emoji reasons — punctuation (`P*`), currency (`Sc`), math (`Sm`) — is still stripped, so baselines like `$4.20B` still normalize as they did (locked by test_currency_symbol_is_still_stripped, and by every existing test that asserts a specific ASCII output).

decisions.question: Why preserve only 'So'/'Sk' and not the wider '\p{S}' set (also 'Sc' currency, 'Sm' math)?
decisions.commitment: Narrow scope, on purpose. Only So (Symbol, other — the emoji block) and Sk (Symbol, modifier — the skin-tone family that composes with emoji base characters) are preserved. Sc ('$', '€', '£') and Sm ('×', '÷', '±', '∞') stay stripped. The Grok peer review sketched the wider version ('regex.sub(r"[^\w\s\p{Emoji}\p{S}]", ...)') as an alternative, and it is a real alternative, but folding it into this PR would silently rekey every baseline like `$4.20B` (currently → `420b`, wide version → `$420b`) and every existing sealed row whose source_text contained a stripped symbol. That is a schema-migration-shaped change requiring its own measurement (which existing rows would rekey? do any baseline benches rely on the pre-fix output?) and its own explicit decision. Deferred as an explicit follow-up. The narrow PR closes the PR #180 finding as filed and leaves the wider question alone until it earns a decision of its own.
decisions.why: The seat rule: 'Don't add features, refactor, or introduce abstractions beyond what the task requires. Three similar lines is better than a premature abstraction.' The task at hand — PR #180's emoji finding — is closed by preserving So/Sk. Widening to Sc/Sm addresses a related class (∞ still collapses; two ∞-only rows still collide) but changes the meaning of every stored row that contains a stripped symbol. That is a bigger question with its own answer path: measure which real deployments' baselines contain currency in the label (not the value — the value is parsed by NumericMatcher, not compared as a string), decide whether the wider preservation is worth the migration, land it separately with its own bench and decision. The ∞-case-still-collapses test in tests/test_matcher_emoji.py locks the limitation so a later PR that widens sees the test fire and knows a decision has to move first.

decisions.question: Should a source that normalizes to '' be refused as a seal, as a safety net against future edge cases?
decisions.commitment: Deferred. The Grok peer review named this as Direction C — an orthogonal safety net that would refuse (or explicitly raise on) any seal whose normalize output is the empty string, so a future collision-prone class cannot silently overwrite. This PR does not add it. Reasons: (a) empty-string sources are already legitimately used in some tests and possibly in some deployments as 'no source, only target' seals; refusing them is a semantics change requiring its own audit and decision; (b) with the emoji fix in place, the concretely-known collision class is closed, so the safety net is not gating this PR; (c) folding this into an emoji-fix PR would obscure whether a downstream regression was caused by the emoji change or the empty-norm refusal. The class of remaining collision-prone inputs (pure Sm like '∞', pure Sc like '$', pure P like '...') would each be closed either by the wider strip-preservation decision above or by this empty-norm refusal — the two options are not exclusive; a later PR can adopt either or both.
decisions.why: The narrow PR closes the specific finding PR #180 filed with the exact test cases PR #180 wrote. Adding an orthogonal safety net inside the same PR would trade a small, clean, easily-reviewed change for a wider one whose regression surface a reviewer would have to unravel. The safety net is a good idea, credited to the peer review, and named here explicitly so a later PR opens the question with the frame already in place. The narrow PR does not close the wider class of collisions; the two follow-up decisions (widen strip, refuse empty) are named so they can be picked up on their own merits.
